preamble: Backing and rounding of the nasalized open vowel [ã] to open-mid [ɔ̃], keeping nasality. In Old Polish the single nasal vowel /ã/ that resulted from the 14th-century merger of Proto-Slavic *ę and *ǫ kept a length contrast. In the 15th century the long member was backed and rounded to /ɔ̃/ and lost its length, giving modern ⟨ą⟩, while the short member was fronted to /ɛ̃/ (⟨ę⟩). This is the source of alternations such as ząb 'tooth' : zęba (gen. sg.).

examples.from: Old Polish long nasal /ãː/ (< Proto-Slavic *ǫ in *zǫ̑bъ 'tooth')
examples.to: ząb 'tooth', with ą /ɔ̃/ (modern /zɔmp/, decomposed before a stop)
examples.note: In the 15th century the short nasal was fronted to [ɛ̃] (ę) and the long one was backed to [ɒ̃~ɔ̃] (ą) and lost its length. That is why ą and ę alternate within one paradigm, as in ząb 'tooth' vs. gen. sg. zęba and nom. pl. zęby. Modern ą is decomposed: [ɔm] before labial stops (hence /zɔmp/) and [ɔw̃] before fricatives.

examples.from: Old Polish long nasal /ãː/ in mąż 'husband' (< Proto-Slavic *mǫžь)
examples.note: The oblique stem has the short-nasal reflex ę (gen. sg. męża, dim. mężulek).
